claim: Plaques of the amyloid beta (Aβ) peptide are a pathological hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Plaques of the amyloid beta (Aß) peptide are a pathological hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most common form of dementia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, representing consensus understanding of AD pathology.

claim: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia.
source: Plaques of the amyloid beta (Aß) peptide are a pathological hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most common form of dementia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about AD epidemiology.

claim: Mutations in Aβ cause familial forms of AD (fAD).
source: Mutations in Aß also cause familial forms of AD (fAD).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The study quantified the effects of >14,000 mutations on the aggregation of Aβ using deep mutational scanning.
source: Here, we use deep mutational scanning to quantify the effects of >14,000 mutations on the aggregation of Aß.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Charge and gatekeeper residues in the disordered region outside of the amyloid core are important in preventing nucleation.
source: The resulting genetic landscape reveals mechanistic insights into fibril nucleation, including the importance of charge and gatekeeper residues in the disordered region outside of the amyloid core in preventing nucleation.
evidence: This is a primary finding derived from the deep mutational scanning data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The empirical nucleation scores accurately identify all known dominant fAD mutations in Aβ.
source: Strikingly, unlike computational predictors and previous measurements, the empirical nucleation scores accurately identify all known dominant fAD mutations in Aß
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the ROC curve analysis showing AUC=0.9 for fAD mutation classification.

claim: Computational predictors and previous measurements do not accurately identify all known dominant fAD mutations in Aβ.
source: Strikingly, unlike computational predictors and previous measurements, the empirical nucleation scores accurately identify all known dominant fAD mutations in Aß
evidence: This is supported by comparison data showing lower AUC values for computational predictors (Figure 4).

claim: The mechanism of nucleation in the cell-based assay is likely to be very similar to the mechanism that causes human fAD.
source: genetically validating that the mechanism of nucleation in a cell-based assay is likely to be very similar to the mechanism that causes the human disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the accurate classification of all known fAD mutations by the nucleation scores.

claim: This is the first comprehensive atlas of how mutations alter the formation of any amyloid fibril.
source: These results provide the first comprehensive atlas of how mutations alter the formation of any amyloid fibril and a resource for the interpretation of genetic variation in Aß.
evidence: This is stated as a primary contribution of the work.

claim: Most cases of AD are sporadic and of uncertain cause.
source: Although most cases of AD are sporadic and of uncertain cause, rare familial forms of the disease also exist (Campion et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Rare familial forms of AD exist.
source: Although most cases of AD are sporadic and of uncertain cause, rare familial forms of the disease also exist (Campion et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Inherited forms of dementia typically have earlier onset.
source: These inherited forms of dementia typically have earlier onset and are caused by high penetrance mutations in multiple loci, including in the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene, which encodes the protein from which Aß is derived by proteolytic cleavage (O'Brien and Wong, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Inherited forms of dementia are caused by high penetrance mutations in multiple loci, including in the APP gene.
source: These inherited forms of dementia typically have earlier onset and are caused by high penetrance mutations in multiple loci, including in the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene, which encodes the protein from which Aß is derived by proteolytic cleavage (O'Brien and Wong, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: APP encodes the protein from which Aβ is derived by proteolytic cleavage.
source: including in the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene, which encodes the protein from which Aß is derived by proteolytic cleavage (O'Brien and Wong, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Several mutations in PSEN1 and PSEN2 lead to autosomal dominant forms of AD.
source: Several mutations in PSEN1 and PSEN2, the genes coding for the secretases performing sequential cleavage of APP, also lead to autosomal dominant forms of AD.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about genetic causes of AD.

claim: PSEN1 and PSEN2 code for the secretases performing sequential cleavage of APP.
source: Several mutations in PSEN1 and PSEN2, the genes coding for the secretases performing sequential cleavage of APP, also lead to autosomal dominant forms of AD.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the function of these genes.

claim: The two most abundant isoforms of Aβ generated upon cleavage are 42 and 40 amino acids in length.
source: The two most abundant isoforms of Aß generated upon cleavage are 42 and 40 amino acids (aa) in length, with the longer Aß peptide associated with increased aggregation in vitro and cellular toxicity (Meisl et al., 2014; Sandberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The longer Aβ peptide (Aβ42) is associated with increased aggregation in vitro and cellular toxicity.
source: The two most abundant isoforms of Aß generated upon cleavage are 42 and 40 amino acids (aa) in length, with the longer Aß peptide associated with increased aggregation in vitro and cellular toxicity (Meisl et al., 2014; Sandberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The amyloid state is a thermodynamically low energy state.
source: The amyloid state is a thermodynamically low energy state but, both in vitro and in vivo, the spontaneous formation of amyloids is normally very slow because of the high kinetic barrier of fibril nucleation (Knowles et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The spontaneous formation of amyloids is normally very slow because of the high kinetic barrier of fibril nucleation.
source: The amyloid state is a thermodynamically low energy state but, both in vitro and in vivo, the spontaneous formation of amyloids is normally very slow because of the high kinetic barrier of fibril nucleation (Knowles et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The process of nucleation generates oligomeric Aβ species that have been hypothesized to be particularly toxic to cells.
source: The process of nucleation generates oligomeric Aß species that have been hypothesized to be particularly toxic to cells and that then grow into fibrils (Michaels et al., 2020; Bolognesi et al., 2010; Cleary et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis from the literature with citation support.

claim: Oligomeric Aβ species grow into fibrils.
source: The process of nucleation generates oligomeric Aß species that have been hypothesized to be particularly toxic to cells and that then grow into fibrils (Michaels et al., 2020; Bolognesi et al., 2010; Cleary et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Fourteen different mutations in the Aβ peptide have been reported to cause familial Alzheimer's disease (fAD).
source: Fourteen different mutations in the Aß peptide have been reported to cause familial Alzheimer's disease (fAD), with all but two having a dominant pattern of inheritance (Weggen and Beher, 2012; Van Cauwenberghe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: All but two fAD mutations in Aβ have a dominant pattern of inheritance.
source: Fourteen different mutations in the Aß peptide have been reported to cause familial Alzheimer's disease (fAD), with all but two having a dominant pattern of inheritance (Weggen and Beher, 2012; Van Cauwenberghe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: It is not clear why particular mutations in Aβ cause fAD.
source: However, it is not clear why these particular mutations cause fAD (Weggen and Beher, 2012; Van Cauwenberghe et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap with citation support.

claim: The 14 known fAD mutations represent only 3.7% of the possible 378 single nucleotide changes that can occur in Aβ.
source: and these 14 mutations represent only 3.7% of the possible 378 single nucleotide changes that can occur in Aß.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the number of known mutations and possible single nucleotide variants.

claim: The molecular mechanism by which mutations cause AD remains unclear for nearly all disease genes.
source: As for nearly all disease genes, therefore, the molecular mechanism by which mutations cause the disease remains unclear and the vast majority of possible mutations in Aß are variants of uncertain significance (VUS).
evidence: This is stated as a general knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The vast majority of possible mutations in Aβ are variants of uncertain significance (VUS).
source: As for nearly all disease genes, therefore, the molecular mechanism by which mutations cause the disease remains unclear and the vast majority of possible mutations in Aß are variants of uncertain significance (VUS).
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that only 14 mutations are known to cause disease out of 378 possible.

claim: Clinical interpretation of genetic variation in Aβ is a difficult challenge.
source: This makes the clinical interpretation of genetic variation in this locus a difficult challenge (Starita et al., 2017; Gelman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the large number of VUS, with citation support.

claim: Nearly all possible variants in Aβ likely exist in at least one individual currently alive on the planet.
source: Moreover, given the human mutation rate and population size, it is likely that nearly all of these possible variants in Aß actually exist in at least one individual currently alive on the planet (Conrad et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from human mutation rate and population size data, with citation support.

claim: A comprehensive map of how all possible mutations affect the formation of Aβ amyloids and how these changes relate to human disease is urgently needed.
source: A comprehensive map of how all possible mutations affect the formation of Aß amyloids and how these changes relate to the human disease is therefore urgently needed.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study based on the identified knowledge gaps.

claim: Amyloid fibrils are associated with many different human diseases.
source: More generally, amyloid fibrils are associated with many different human diseases (Knowles et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: How mutations alter the propensity of proteins to aggregate into amyloid fibrils is not well understood.
source: but how mutations alter the propensity of proteins to aggregate into amyloid fibrils is not well understood and there has been no large-scale analysis of the effects of mutations on the formation of any amyloid fibril.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: There has been no large-scale analysis of the effects of mutations on the formation of any amyloid fibril prior to this study.
source: but how mutations alter the propensity of proteins to aggregate into amyloid fibrils is not well understood and there has been no large-scale analysis of the effects of mutations on the formation of any amyloid fibril.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The study quantified the rate of fibril formation for >14,000 variants of Aβ.
source: Here, we address this shortcoming by quantifying the rate of fibril formation for >14,000 variants of Aß.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The data accurately classify all the known dominant fAD mutations.
source: Moreover, they also accurately classify all the known dominant fAD mutations, validating the clinical relevance of a simple cell-based model and providing a comprehensive resource for the interpretation of clinical genetic data.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the ROC curve analysis.

claim: The study validates the clinical relevance of a simple cell-based model.
source: Moreover, they also accurately classify all the known dominant fAD mutations, validating the clinical relevance of a simple cell-based model and providing a comprehensive resource for the interpretation of clinical genetic data.
evidence: This is inferred from the accurate classification of fAD mutations.

claim: The study used an in vivo selection assay in which the nucleation of Aβ is rate-limiting for the aggregation of the yeast prion [PSI+].
source: To globally quantify the impact of mutations on the nucleation of Aß fibrils, we used an in vivo selection assay in which the nucleation of Aß is rate-limiting for the aggregation of a second amyloid, the yeast prion [PSI+] encoded by the sup35 gene (Chandramowlishwaran et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study, with citation support.

claim: Aggregation of Sup35p causes read-through of UGA stop codons.
source: Aggregation of Sup35p causes read-through of UGA stop codons, allowing growth-based selection using an auxotrophic marker containing a premature termination codon (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the selection assay, with reference to figures.

claim: The study generated a library containing all possible single nucleotide variants of Aβ42 fused to the nucleation (N) domain of Sup35p.
source: We generated a library containing all possible single nucleotide variants of Aß42 fused to the nucleation (N) domain of Sup35p and quantified the effect of mutations on the rate of nucleation in triplicate by selection and deep sequencing (Faure et al., 2020; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The selection assay was highly reproducible.
source: The selection assay was highly reproducible, with enrichment scores for aa substitutions strongly correlated between replicates (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation data shown in the figures.

claim: Enrichment scores for amino acid substitutions were strongly correlated between replicates.
source: The selection assay was highly reproducible, with enrichment scores for aa substitutions strongly correlated between replicates (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with Pearson correlation coefficient R=0.85, p<2.2e-16.

claim: The in vivo enrichment scores match the effects on in vitro nucleation previously reported for 14 out of 16 Aβ variants.
source: Comparing our in vivo enrichment scores to the qualitative effects of 16 mutations analysed in vitro across 10 previous publications validated the assay, with mutational effects matching the effects on in vitro nucleation previously reported for 14 Aß variants out of 16. (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a validation of the assay by comparison to published data.

claim: The in vivo scores correlate extremely well with the rate of nucleation of Aβ variants in positions 21, 22, 23.
source: Moreover, the in vivo scores correlate extremely well with the rate of nucleation of Aß variants in positions 21, 22, 23 (Yang et al., 2018; Törnquist et al., 2018; Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with high correlation coefficients for primary and secondary nucleation.

claim: Solubility scores from a prior deep mutational scan do not predict the effects of mutations on Aβ nucleation.
source: A prior deep mutational scan quantified the effects of mutations on the abundance of Aß fused to an enzymatic reporter (Gray et al., 2019). These 'solubility scores' do not predict the effects of mutations on Aß nucleation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by lack of correlation in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PC1 (related to changes in hydrophobicity) is not a good predictor of Aβ nucleation.
source: PC1 is also not a good predictor of Aß nucleation (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with weak correlation (R=0.2).

claim: PC1 predicts the previously reported changes in Aβ solubility.
source: but it does predict the previously reported changes in Aß solubility (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E with strong negative correlation (R=-0.82).

claim: Aβ is aggregating by a similar process to TDP-43 in the alternative selection assay but by a different mechanism in the nucleation selection.
source: suggesting that Aß is aggregating by a similar process to TDP-43 in this alternative selection assay (Gray et al., 2019) but by a different mechanism in the nucleation selection.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential predictive power of PC1 for solubility vs. nucleation scores.

claim: 56% of single amino acid substitutions reduce nucleation.
source: The distribution of mutational effects for Aß nucleation has a strong bias towards reduced nucleation, with 56% of single aa substitutions reducing nucleation but only 16% increasing it (Z-test, false discovery rate [FDR] = 0.1, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the deep mutational scanning data.

claim: Only 16% of single amino acid substitutions increase nucleation.
source: The distribution of mutational effects for Aß nucleation has a strong bias towards reduced nucleation, with 56% of single aa substitutions reducing nucleation but only 16% increasing it (Z-test, false discovery rate [FDR] = 0.1, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the deep mutational scanning data.

claim: Mutations that decrease nucleation typically have a larger effect than those that increase it.
source: Moreover, mutations that decrease nucleation in our dataset typically have a larger effect than those that increase it, with many mutations reducing nucleation to the background rate observed for Aß variants containing premature termination codons (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the distribution of nucleation scores shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The study quantified the impact of 14,015 double amino acid variants of Aβ.
source: In total, we quantified the impact of 14,015 double aa variants of Aß.
evidence: This is a primary finding describing the scope of the study.

claim: 63% of double mutants decrease nucleation and only 5.5% increase nucleation.
source: Double mutants were even more likely to reduce nucleation, with 63% decreasing and only 5.5% increasing nucleation (Z-test, FDR = 0.1; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the deep mutational scanning data.

claim: Mutations more frequently decrease rather than increase Aβ nucleation.
source: Therefore, mutations more frequently decrease rather than increase Aß nucleation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the distribution of mutational effects for both single and double mutants.

claim: Mutations that decrease nucleation are highly enriched in the C-terminus of Aβ.
source: Mutations that decrease nucleation are highly enriched in the C-terminus of Aß, whereas mutations that increase nucleation are enriched in the N-terminus (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E and is a primary finding about the spatial distribution of mutational effects.

claim: Mutations that increase nucleation are enriched in the N-terminus of Aβ.
source: Mutations that decrease nucleation are highly enriched in the C-terminus of Aß, whereas mutations that increase nucleation are enriched in the N-terminus (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E and is a primary finding about the spatial distribution of mutational effects.

claim: >84% of mutations in the C-terminus (residues 27-42) reduce nucleation and only 9.6% increase it.
source: Indeed, >84% of mutations in the C-terminus (residues 27-42) reduce nucleation and only 9.6% increase it (FDR = 0.1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the deep mutational scanning data.

claim: The effects of mutations are smaller and more balanced in the first 26 amino acids of the peptide.
source: In contrast, the effects of mutations are smaller (Figure 2F) and also more balanced in the first 26 aa of the peptide, with 38.6% decreasing and 20% increasing nucleation (FDR = 0.1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F and is a primary finding about regional differences in mutational effects.

claim: 38.6% of mutations in the first 26 amino acids decrease nucleation and 20% increase it.
source: In contrast, the effects of mutations are smaller (Figure 2F) and also more balanced in the first 26 aa of the peptide, with 38.6% decreasing and 20% increasing nucleation (FDR = 0.1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the deep mutational scanning data.

claim: The differences in mutational effects between the N- and C-terminal regions suggest a modular organization of the peptide.
source: These differences in the direction and strength of mutational effects between the N- and C-terminal regions of Aß suggest a modular organization of the peptide.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in mutational effects between regions.

claim: Aβ has a hydrophobic C-terminus and a more polar and charged N-terminus.
source: This modularity is also reflected in the primary sequence of Aß, which has a hydrophobic C-terminus and a more polar and charged N-terminus (eight out of nine charged residues in Aß are found before residue 24 and the peptide consists entirely of hydrophobic residues from position 29) (Figures 2C and 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the amino acid sequence composition.

claim: Eight out of nine charged residues in Aβ are found before residue 24.
source: This modularity is also reflected in the primary sequence of Aß, which has a hydrophobic C-terminus and a more polar and charged N-terminus (eight out of nine charged residues in Aß are found before residue 24 and the peptide consists entirely of hydrophobic residues from position 29) (Figures 2C and 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the amino acid sequence composition.

claim: The peptide consists entirely of hydrophobic residues from position 29.
source: This modularity is also reflected in the primary sequence of Aß, which has a hydrophobic C-terminus and a more polar and charged N-terminus (eight out of nine charged residues in Aß are found before residue 24 and the peptide consists entirely of hydrophobic residues from position 29) (Figures 2C and 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the amino acid sequence composition.

claim: Mutations in the few hydrophobic residues in the N-terminus have effects more similar to mutations in polar residues in the N-terminus rather than in hydrophobic residues in the C-terminus.
source: Consistent with this modular organization, mutations in the few hydrophobic residues in the N-terminus have effects that are more similar to mutations in polar residues in the N-terminus rather than in hydrophobic residues in the C-terminus.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of mutational effects across different positions.

claim: Mutations in K28 frequently strongly reduce nucleation, just as they do in the adjacent hydrophobic positions.
source: Similarly, mutations in the most C-terminal charged residue (K28) frequently strongly reduce nucleation, just as they do in the adjacent hydrophobic positions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and is a primary finding about position-specific effects.

claim: There are only seven positions in Aβ where mutations are not more likely to decrease rather than increase nucleation.
source: Considering the entire Aß peptide, there are only seven positions in which mutations are not more likely to decrease rather than increase nucleation (FDR = 0.1; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from analysis of the mutational landscape.

claim: The seven gatekeeper positions include five of the six negatively charged residues in Aβ.
source: Strikingly, these positions, which we refer to as 'gatekeepers' of nucleation (Rousseau et al., 2006; Pedersen et al., 2004), include five of the six negatively charged residues in Aß.
evidence: This is a primary finding about the identity of gatekeeper positions.

claim: L17 is a gatekeeper position where seven mutations increase nucleation and only one decreases it.
source: The sixth gatekeeper is an unusual hydrophobic residue in the N-terminus, L17, where seven mutations increase nucleation and only one decreases it (FDR = 0.1; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding about position-specific effects.

claim: A42 has an unusual distribution of mutational effects different from the rest of the C-terminus, with four mutations increasing and three decreasing nucleation.
source: The final aa of the peptide, A42, also has an unusual distribution of mutational effects that is different to the rest of the C-terminus, with four mutations increasing and three mutations decreasing nucleation (FDR = 0.1; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding about position-specific effects.

claim: Mutations in the C-terminus nearly all decrease nucleation.
source: Mutations in the C-terminus nearly all decrease nucleation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and is a primary finding.

claim: The C-terminus forms part of the tightly packed amyloid core of all known structural polymorphs of both Aβ42 and Aβ40.
source: This is consistent with the C-terminus forming part of the tightly packed amyloid core of all known structural polymorphs of both Aß42 (Colvin et al., 2016; Meier et al., 2017; Wälti et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2015; Gremer et al., 2017; Lührs et al., 2005; Schmidt et al., 2015) and Aß40 (Kollmer et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2013; Qiang et al., 2012; Sgourakis et al., 2015; Paravastu et al., 2008; Schütz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from structural studies with extensive citation support.

claim: C-terminal fragments of Aβ (aa 22-42, 24-42, 27-42) nucleate similarly or better than full length Aβ.
source: Consistent with this, we quantified the nucleation of three C-terminal fragments of the peptide (aa 22-42, 24-42, 27-42) and found that they nucleate similarly or better than full length Aß (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental testing of C-terminal fragments.

claim: Mutations to polar and charged residues in the C-terminus nearly all decrease nucleation.
source: Mutations to polar and charged residues in this region nearly all decrease nucleation, but so too do most changes to other hydrophobic residues (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and is a primary finding.

claim: Most changes to hydrophobic residues in the C-terminus decrease nucleation.
source: Mutations to polar and charged residues in this region nearly all decrease nucleation, but so too do most changes to other hydrophobic residues (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and is a primary finding.

claim: Specific side chain packing in the C-terminus is important for nucleation.
source: suggesting specific side chain packing in this region is important for nucleation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most mutations in the C-terminus decrease nucleation.

claim: The relative effects of different mutations in the C-terminus are only partially captured by changes in hydrophobicity.
source: The relative effects of different mutations are only partially captured by changes in hydrophobicity (Figure 3F; Pearson correlation coefficient, R = 0.45)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F with moderate correlation.

claim: Only a few mutations in the C-terminus increase nucleation: substitutions to isoleucine at positions 30, 34, and 39; mutations to valine at positions 29, 30, and 34; a change to threonine at position 30; changes to leucine and methionine at 36; and a mutation to phenylalanine at position 41.
source: Only a few mutations in this region increase nucleation: substitutions to isoleucine at positions 30, 34, and 39; mutations to valine at positions 29, 30, and 34; a change to threonine at position 30; changes to leucine and methionine at 36; and a mutation to phenylalanine at position 41 (FDR = 0.1).
evidence: This is a primary finding identifying specific mutations that increase nucleation in the C-terminus.

claim: Mutations in the N-terminus of Aβ have a more balanced effect on nucleation.
source: Mutations in the N-terminus of Aß have a more balanced effect on nucleation
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing N-terminal to C-terminal mutational effects.

claim: The effects of mutations in the N-terminus are not well predicted by hydrophobicity or predictors of aggregation potential.
source: and these effects are not well predicted by either hydrophobicity or predictors of aggregation potential (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,D and E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,D and E with weak correlations.

claim: The introduction of asparagine, isoleucine, and valine in the N-terminus is most likely to increase nucleation.
source: The effects of introducing particular aa are, however, biased, with the introduction of asparagine, isoleucine, and valine most likely to increase nucleation (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and is a primary finding about amino acid-specific effects.

claim: The introduction of negative charged residues in the N-terminus typically strongly reduces nucleation.
source: As at the C-terminus, the introduction of negative charged residues typically strongly reduces nucleation (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3B and C and is a primary finding.

claim: The effects of introducing positive charge in the N-terminus are less severe than in the C-terminus.
source: However, in contrast to what is observed in the C-terminus (Figure 3B), the effects of introducing positive charge are less severe (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: The effects of mutations to proline, isoleucine, valine, and threonine in the N-terminus depend on the position: mutations in the first 12 residues typically decrease nucleation, whereas mutations in the next four to nine residues increase nucleation.
source: Interestingly, the effects of mutations to proline, isoleucine, valine, and threonine in the N-terminus depend on the position in which they are made: mutations in the first 12 residues typically decrease nucleation, whereas mutations in the next four to nine residues increase nucleation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E and is a primary finding about position-dependent effects.

claim: The conformational rigidity of proline and the beta-branched side chains of isoleucine, valine, and threonine disfavour helix formation.
source: The conformational rigidity of proline and the beta-branched side chains of isoleucine, valine, and threonine that disfavour helix formation suggest that disruption of a secondary structure in this region may favour nucleation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about amino acid properties.

claim: Disruption of a secondary structure in the N-terminal region (residues 13-21) may favour nucleation.
source: The conformational rigidity of proline and the beta-branched side chains of isoleucine, valine, and threonine that disfavour helix formation suggest that disruption of a secondary structure in this region may favour nucleation.
evidence: This is inferred from the position-dependent effects of structure-disrupting amino acids.

claim: The region around residues 13-21 was highlighted as the part of the peptide remaining most disordered across different states of the solution ensemble of Aβ in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Interestingly, this same region was highlighted as the part of the peptide remaining most disordered across different states of the solution ensemble of Aß in molecular dynamics simulations, with the same region also making extensive long-range contacts in different states of the kinetic ensemble (Löhr et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from a molecular dynamics simulation study.

claim: At five of six negatively charged positions in Aβ, mutations frequently increase nucleation.
source: At five of six negatively charged positions in Aß, mutations frequently increase nucleation (Figures 2D and 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2D and 3A and is a primary finding.

claim: The introduction of negative charge at other positions strongly decreases nucleation.
source: Moreover, the introduction of negative charge at other positions strongly decreases nucleation (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and is a primary finding.

claim: Negatively charged residues act as gatekeepers to limit nucleation.
source: suggesting that negatively charged residues act as gatekeepers (Pedersen et al., 2004; Rousseau et al., 2006) to limit nucleation (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational effects at negatively charged positions, with citation to the gatekeeper concept.

claim: Mutations in the three positively charged residues (R5, K16, K28) mostly decrease nucleation.
source: In contrast, mutations in the three positively charged residues (R5, K16, K28) mostly decrease nucleation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and is a primary finding.

claim: Mutating negatively charged gatekeepers to glutamine, asparagine, positively charged residues, or small side chains increases nucleation.
source: Mutating the negatively charged gatekeepers to the polar aa glutamine and asparagine, to positively charged residues (arginine and lysine), or to small side chains (glycine and alanine) increases nucleation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and is a primary finding.

claim: Mutating negatively charged gatekeepers to hydrophobic residues typically reduces nucleation.
source: Mutating the same positions to hydrophobic residues typically reduces nucleation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and is a primary finding.

claim: The negative charge at gatekeeper positions acts to limit nucleation, but the overall polar and unstructured nature of the N-terminus must be maintained for effective nucleation.
source: This is consistent with a model in which the negative charge at these positions acts to limit nucleation, but that the overall polar and unstructured nature of the N-terminus must be maintained for effective nucleation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from the mutational effects at gatekeeper positions.

claim: Reducing the net charge of the peptide from −3 progressively increases nucleation.
source: Considering all mutations between charged and polar residues or glycine reveals that, although reducing the net charge of the peptide from −3 progressively increases nucleation (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G and is a primary finding from analysis of double mutants.

claim: For a given net charge, nucleation is increased in peptides containing fewer charged residues of any sign.
source: the total number of charged residues is also important: for a given net charge, nucleation is increased in peptides containing fewer charged residues of any sign (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G and is a primary finding.

claim: Both the overall charge and the number of charged residues control the rate of Aβ nucleation.
source: Thus, both the overall charge and the number of charged residues control the rate of Aß nucleation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of charge effects on nucleation.

claim: At position 17, changes to polar, aromatic, and aliphatic amino acids all increase nucleation, as does the introduction of a positive charge and mutation to proline.
source: At position 17, changes to polar, aromatic, and aliphatic aa all increase nucleation, as does the introduction of a positive charge and mutation to proline.
evidence: This is a primary finding about position-specific effects at L17.

claim: Only a mutation to cysteine at position 17 reduces nucleation.
source: Only a mutation to cysteine reduces nucleation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and is a primary finding.

claim: Leucine at position 17 has a specific role in limiting nucleation.
source: This suggests a specific role for leucine at position 17 in limiting nucleation, perhaps as part of a nucleation-limiting secondary structure suggested by the mutational effects of proline, isoleucine, valine, and threonine in this region (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational effects at position 17.

claim: Mutations at position 42 most often increase nucleation.
source: Finally, the distribution of mutational effects at position 42 differs from that in the rest of the hydrophobic C-terminus of Aß, with mutations most often increasing nucleation (Figure 2D; FDR = 0.1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and is a primary finding.

claim: The mutations that increase nucleation at position 42 are all to other aliphatic residues.
source: The mutations that increase nucleation are all to other aliphatic residues (Figures 2C and 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2C and 3A and is a primary finding.

claim: Aβ42 has increased toxicity and aggregation propensity compared to Aβ40.
source: The distinction of position 42 is interesting because of the increased toxicity and aggregation propensity of Aß42 compared to the shorter Aß40 APP cleavage product (Meisl et al., 2014; Sandberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: There are 11 mutations in Aβ reported to cause dominantly inherited fAD and one additional variant of unclear pathogenicity (H6R).
source: In total, there are 11 mutations in Aß reported to cause dominantly inherited fAD and one additional variant of unclear pathogenicity (H6R) (Janssen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The 12 known disease mutations are not well discriminated by commonly used computational variant effect predictors.
source: These 12 known disease mutations are not well discriminated by commonly used computational variant effect predictors (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A with low AUC values.

claim: The 12 known disease mutations are not well discriminated by computational predictors of protein aggregation and solubility.
source: or by computational predictors of protein aggregation and solubility (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B with low AUC values.

claim: The 12 known disease mutations are poorly predicted by the previous deep mutational scan of Aβ designed to quantify changes in protein solubility.
source: They are also poorly predicted by the previous deep mutational scan of Aß designed to quantify changes in protein solubility, suggesting the disease is unrelated to the biophysical process quantified in this assay (Gray et al., 2019; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C with AUC=0.5.

claim: The disease is unrelated to the biophysical process quantified in the solubility assay.
source: They are also poorly predicted by the previous deep mutational scan of Aß designed to quantify changes in protein solubility, suggesting the disease is unrelated to the biophysical process quantified in this assay (Gray et al., 2019; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the poor prediction of fAD mutations by solubility scores.

claim: The nucleation scores accurately classify the known dominant fAD mutations, with all 12 mutations increasing nucleation.
source: In contrast, the scores from our in vivo nucleation assay accurately classify the known dominant fAD mutations, with all 12 mutations increasing nucleation (Figure 4, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, ROC−AUC = 0.9, two-tailed Z-test, p<2.2e-16).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with ROC-AUC = 0.9 and is a primary finding.

claim: The biophysical events occurring in the cell-based assay are highly relevant to the development of human fAD.
source: This suggests the biophysical events occurring in this simple cell-based assay are highly relevant to the development of the human disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the accurate classification of fAD mutations.

claim: The known fAD mutations are enriched in the N-terminus of Aβ.
source: Consistent with the overall mutational landscape, the known fAD mutations are also enriched in the N-terminus of Aß (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and is a primary finding.

claim: K16N is likely to be one of only two fAD mutations in position 16.
source: For example, based on our data, K16N is likely to be one of only two fAD mutations in position 16.
evidence: This is inferred from the nucleation scores at position 16.

claim: At position 11, there are five mutations with a nucleation score higher than the known E11K disease mutation.
source: However, in other positions, there are several additional variants that increase nucleation as much as the known fAD mutation. At position 11, for example, there are five mutations with a NS higher than the known E11K disease mutation (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2C and D and is a primary finding.

claim: There are likely to be many additional dominant fAD mutations beyond the 12 that have been reported to date.
source: Overall, our data suggest there are likely to be many additional dominant fAD mutations beyond the 12 that have been reported to date (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of 63 candidate fAD variants.

claim: Two additional variants in Aβ (E22Δ and A2V) have been suggested to act recessively to cause fAD.
source: In addition to the 12 known dominant fAD mutations, two additional variants in Aß have been suggested to act recessively to cause fAD (Di Fede et al., 2009; Tomiyama et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: E22Δ is a codon deletion and is not present in the study library.
source: One of these variants is a codon deletion (E22Δ) and is not present in our library.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: A2V does not have a dominant effect on nucleation in the assay.
source: The other variant, A2V, does not have a dominant effect on nucleation in our assay (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and is a primary finding.

claim: A2V is consistent with a recessive pattern of inheritance and a different mechanism of action, such as reduced β-cleavage and increased Aβ42 generation.
source: consistent with a recessive pattern of inheritance and a different mechanism of action, such as reduced ß-cleavage and increased Aß42 generation, as previously proposed (Benilova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of dominant effect and cited from previous work.

claim: The data prioritize 63 variants as candidate fAD variants.
source: More generally, of the hundreds of aa changes possible in the peptide, our data prioritize 63 as candidate fAD variants (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of nucleation scores.

claim: 131 variants are likely to be benign.
source: 131 variants are likely to be benign
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of nucleation scores.

claim: 262 variants reduce Aβ nucleation and may be protective.
source: and 262 reduce Aß nucleation and so may even be protective.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of nucleation scores.

claim: No correlation was observed between nucleation scores and disease age-of-onset with the currently available data.
source: With the currently available data for patients carrying fAD mutations, we could not observe a correlation between NS and disease age-of-onset (Ryman et al., 2014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and is a primary finding.

claim: A majority of mutations in the C-terminal core of Aβ disrupt nucleation.
source: A majority of mutations in the C-terminal core of Aß disrupt nucleation, consistent with specific hydrophobic contacts in this region being required for nucleation.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings from the mutational landscape.

claim: Specific hydrophobic contacts in the C-terminal region are required for nucleation.
source: A majority of mutations in the C-terminal core of Aß disrupt nucleation, consistent with specific hydrophobic contacts in this region being required for nucleation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most mutations in the C-terminus disrupt nucleation.

claim: Mutations that increase nucleation are enriched in the polar N-terminus with mutations in negatively charged gatekeeper residues and the L17 gatekeeper being particularly likely to accelerate aggregation.
source: In contrast, mutations that increase nucleation are enriched in the polar N-terminus with mutations in negatively charged gatekeeper residues and the L17 gatekeeper being particularly likely to accelerate aggregation.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings from the mutational landscape.

claim: Decreasing both the net charge of the peptide and the total number of charged residues increases nucleation.
source: Indeed, decreasing both the net charge of the peptide and the total number of charged residues increases nucleation.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings about charge effects.

claim: Little is known about the structure of Aβ during fibril nucleation.
source: Little is known about the structure of Aß during fibril nucleation
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The results are consistent with the nucleation transition state resembling the known mature fibril structures of Aβ where the C-terminal region is in the amyloid core and the N-terminus is disordered and solvent exposed.
source: but the results presented here are in general consistent with the nucleation transition state resembling the known mature fibril structures of Aß where the C-terminal region of the peptide is located in the amyloid core and the N-terminus is disordered and solvent exposed (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of mutational effects to known fibril structures.

claim: The N-terminus is not required for nucleation.
source: Although the N-terminus is not required for nucleation, it does affect the process when present and most mutations that accelerate nucleation are located in the N-terminus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that C-terminal fragments can nucleate.

claim: The N-terminus affects the nucleation process when present.
source: Although the N-terminus is not required for nucleation, it does affect the process when present and most mutations that accelerate nucleation are located in the N-terminus.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational effects in the N-terminus.

claim: Most mutations that accelerate nucleation are located in the N-terminus.
source: Although the N-terminus is not required for nucleation, it does affect the process when present and most mutations that accelerate nucleation are located in the N-terminus.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mutational landscape.

claim: The effects of mutations in residues immediately before position 17 suggest that the formation of a structural element in this region may interfere with nucleation.
source: Interestingly, the effects of mutations in residues immediately before position 17 suggest that the formation of a structural element in this region may interfere with nucleation.
evidence: This is inferred from the position-dependent effects of structure-disrupting mutations.

claim: Accelerated nucleation is a common cause of fAD.
source: That accelerated nucleation is a common cause of fAD is also supported by the effects of mutations in APP outside of Aß and by the effects of mutations in PSEN1 and PSEN2.
evidence: This is inferred from the accurate classification of fAD mutations and supported by knowledge of other fAD mutations.

claim: Mutations in APP outside of Aβ and mutations in PSEN1 and PSEN2 destabilise enzyme-substrate complexes, increasing the production of longer Aβ peptides that more effectively nucleate amyloid formation.
source: These mutations destabilise enzyme-substrate complexes, increasing the production of the longer Aß peptides that more effectively nucleates amyloid formation (Szaruga et al., 2017; Veugelen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Aβ42 oligomers are hypothesised to be more toxic.
source: In addition, Aß42 oligomers are hypothesised to be more toxic (Michaels et al., 2020; Bolognesi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis from the literature with citation support.

claim: The effects of some mutations on nucleation may be mediated by a change in the concentration of Aβ rather than by an increase in a kinetic rate parameter.
source: It is possible that the effects of some of the mutations reported here on nucleation are also mediated by a change in the concentration of Aß rather than by an increase in a kinetic rate parameter.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Some of the variants evaluated may have additional effects, such as altering cleavage of APP.
source: Some of the variants evaluated here may have additional effects, for example, altering cleavage of APP.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about additional mechanisms.

claim: In yeast, Aβ can aggregate in at least two different ways.
source: Comparing our results to the effects of mutations on Aß solubility quantified in a previous high-throughput analysis (Gray et al., 2019) provides evidence that, in the same type of cell (yeast), Aß can aggregate in at least two different ways.
evidence: This is inferred from the different predictive power of the two assays for fAD mutations.

claim: One aggregation process (quantified by the nucleation assay) is likely to be very similar to the aggregation that occurs in the human brain in fAD.
source: Moreover, the different performance of the two sets of scores from these datasets in classifying fAD mutations suggests that one of these aggregation processes (quantified by the nucleation assay employed here) is likely to be very similar to the aggregation that occurs in the human brain in fAD.
evidence: This is inferred from the accurate classification of fAD mutations by nucleation scores.

claim: The other pathway of aggregation (quantified by the solubility assay) is less obviously related to the human disease.
source: The other pathway of aggregation (quantified by the solubility assay; Gray et al., 2019), however, is less obviously related to the human disease, because mutations that cause fAD do not consistently affect it.
evidence: This is inferred from the poor prediction of fAD mutations by solubility scores.

claim: The second aggregation pathway is driven by changes in hydrophobicity, similar to the aggregation of TDP-43 in yeast.
source: This second aggregation pathway is, at least to a large extent, driven by changes in hydrophobicity, similar to what we previously reported for the aggregation in yeast of the ALS protein, TDP-43 (Bolognesi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation of solubility scores with PC1 (hydrophobicity).

claim: The combination of deep mutational scanning and human genetics can be a general 'genetic' strategy to quantify the disease relevance of biological assays.
source: More generally, our results highlight how the combination of deep mutational scanning and human genetics can be a general 'genetic' strategy to quantify the disease relevance of biological assays.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's approach and results.

claim: The yeast-based assay is better validated as a model of fAD than many other models, including animal models where only one or a few mutations have been tested.
source: Indeed, one could argue that this simple system is now better validated as a model of fAD than many others, including animal models where the effects of only one or a few mutations (including control mutations) have ever been tested.
evidence: This is argued based on the comprehensive genetic validation of the assay.

claim: The combination of deep mutational scanning and human genetics provides a general strategy to quantify the disease relevance of in vitro and cell-based assays.
source: We suggest therefore that the combination of deep mutational scanning and human genetics provides a general strategy to quantify the disease relevance of in vitro and cell-based assays.
evidence: This is a general conclusion and recommendation based on the study's approach.

claim: Deep mutagenesis should be employed early in discovery programmes to 'genetically validate' the relevance of assays for particular diseases.
source: We encourage that deep mutagenesis should be employed early in discovery programmes to 'genetically validate' (or invalidate) the relevance of assays for particular diseases.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's approach and results.

claim: The concordance between mutational effects in an assay and a disease is an unbiased metric that can be used to prioritize between different assays.
source: The concordance between mutational effects in an assay and a disease is an unbiased metric that can be used to prioritize between different assays.
evidence: This is a general principle derived from the study's approach.

claim: Quantifying the 'genetic agreement' between an assay and a disease will help prevent time and resources being wasted on research that has little relevance to a disease.
source: Quantifying the 'genetic agreement' between an assay and a disease will help prevent time and resources being wasted on research that actually has little relevance to a disease.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the utility of the approach.

claim: The consistent effects of dominant fAD mutations strengthen the evidence that fAD is a 'nucleation disease' ultimately caused by an increased rate of amyloid nucleation.
source: Finally, the strikingly consistent effects of the dominant fAD mutations in our assay further strengthen the evidence that fAD is a 'nucleation disease' ultimately caused by an increased rate of amyloid nucleation (Aprile et al., 2017; Cohen et al., 2018; Knowles et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the accurate classification of fAD mutations and supported by citations.

claim: Accelerated nucleation can be caused by direct effects of mutations in Aβ or by changes in upstream factors.
source: This accelerated nucleation can be caused by the direct effects of mutations in Aß — such as those quantified here — or by changes in upstream factors (Szaruga et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a general principle with citation support.

claim: If fAD is a nucleation disease, then nucleation is the key biophysical step to target to prevent or treat AD.
source: If this hypothesis is correct, then nucleation is the key bioph step to target to prevent or treat AD.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the nucleation disease hypothesis.

claim: 'Genetic validation' of assays by mutational scanning and comparison to sets of known disease-causing mutations will be increasingly important in assay development and drug discovery pipelines.
source: We suggest that the 'genetic validation' of assays by mutational scanning and comparison to sets of known disease-causing mutations will be increasingly important in assay development and drug discovery pipelines.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's approach and results.
